items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.

items.title: Hindu philosophy teaches the unity of atman and Brahman
items.claim: What is the relationship between atman and Brahman in Vedantic Hinduism?

options.text: They are completely separate — the soul and a creator god

The Upanishads teach that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one — 'tat tvam asi' ('that thou art', Chandogya Upanishad). Different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship variously (non-dual, qualified non-dual, dualist)
Atman is illusion; only Brahman is real, with no relation between them
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10) and 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are valid orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.
